summary: Minodronic acid hydrate is an oral nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate approved in Japan (Bonoteo / Recalbon) for the treatment of osteoporosis; it is not FDA-approved (data below are drawn from the Japanese package insert and published literature). It is among the most potent antiresorptive bisphosphonates studied in Japan, inhibiting osteoclast-mediated bone resorption via farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase inhibition, raising lumbar-spine and hip bone mineral density and reducing vertebral fractures. It is taken either as 1 mg daily or 50 mg once every 4 weeks, always on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, remaining upright and fasting for at least 30 minutes to minimize esophageal injury. Because oral bioavailability is markedly reduced by food (especially high-fat meals) and by polyvalent cations, dosing and timing are strict. It is contraindicated in esophageal abnormalities that delay emptying, in patients unable to remain upright for 30 minutes, in uncorrected hypocalcemia, and in pregnancy. Key class risks include esophagitis, hypocalcemia, osteonecrosis of the jaw, and atypical femoral fracture.
indications: Treatment of osteoporosis (including postmenopausal osteoporosis) to increase bone mineral density and reduce fracture risk - Japan/PMDA approved indication

admin: Take first thing in the morning on an empty stomach, before any food, drink, or other oral medicine
Swallow the tablet whole with about 180 mL (a full glass) of plain water - not mineral water, juice, coffee, tea, or milk
Do not chew, suck, or crush the tablet (risk of oropharyngeal/esophageal ulceration)
Remain sitting or standing upright and do not lie down for at least 30 minutes after dosing
Wait at least 30 minutes before eating, drinking anything other than water, or taking other medicines
Separate from calcium, antacids, iron, magnesium and other polyvalent-cation products, which block absorption
Ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D intake unless contraindicated
moa: Minodronic acid is a nitrogen-containing (imidazole-ring) third-generation bisphosphonate. Like other bisphosphonates it binds with high affinity to hydroxyapatite mineral at sites of active bone remodeling. During bone resorption it is internalized by osteoclasts, where it inhibits farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway. This blocks prenylation of small GTP-binding signaling proteins (such as Ras, Rho, Rac) required for osteoclast cytoskeletal organization, ruffled-border formation, and survival, thereby suppressing osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. The net effect is reduced bone turnover, increased bone mineral density, and decreased fracture risk. It is reported to be among the most potent inhibitors of bone resorption among bisphosphonates used in Japan.

absolute: Esophageal abnormalities that delay esophageal emptying (e.g., stricture, achalasia)
Inability to sit or stand upright for at least 30 minutes after dosing
Known hypersensitivity to minodronic acid or any component
relative: Significant renal impairment (drug is renally eliminated; accumulation risk)
Active upper gastrointestinal disease (dysphagia, esophagitis, gastritis, ulcer)
Invasive dental work / poor dental health (osteonecrosis of the jaw risk)
monitor: Serum calcium and vitamin D status before and during therapy
Bone mineral density and bone turnover markers
Oral/dental health and any jaw symptoms
New or unusual thigh, hip, or groin pain (atypical femoral fracture)

preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy. Bisphosphonates cross the placenta and are incorporated into the fetal skeleton, with potential for skeletal and other adverse effects shown in animals; there are no adequate human data and the drug has a very long skeletal retention. Avoid in women who are or may become pregnant.
lact: Use is not recommended during breastfeeding. It is not established whether minodronic acid is excreted in human milk; because of bisphosphonate skeletal retention and unknown infant risk, avoid or discontinue nursing during therapy.
renal: Minodronic acid is eliminated principally by the kidneys, so it can accumulate when renal function is reduced; exposure is also higher in the elderly, partly reflecting reduced renal function. Use with caution and consider avoiding in patients with significant renal impairment. Per the Japanese label, severe renal impairment warrants careful risk assessment as clinical data are limited.
hepatic: Minodronic acid is not metabolized by the liver (it is excreted essentially unchanged in urine), so hepatic impairment is not expected to require dose adjustment. No specific hepatic dosing recommendation is provided.

moderate: Polyvalent cations - calcium, magnesium, aluminum, and iron supplements/antacids markedly reduce oral absorption; separate dosing
Other drugs that injure the upper GI mucosa (e.g., NSAIDs) may increase esophageal/gastric adverse effects
minor: No clinically significant cytochrome P450-mediated metabolic interactions (renally excreted, not hepatically metabolized)
interactions.food: Food markedly reduces absorption; a high-fat breakfast lowered Cmax by about 55% and AUC by about 72% versus fasting. Always take on an empty stomach with plain water only.
interactions.alcohol: No direct pharmacokinetic interaction, but heavy alcohol use worsens bone loss and upper-GI irritation; moderate intake.
interactions.diagnostics: May lower bone turnover markers (e.g., urinary NTx, deoxypyridinoline, serum bone-specific alkaline phosphatase, osteocalcin); no characteristic assay interference.

common: Upper gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, dyspepsia, epigastric/abdominal discomfort)
rare: Hypersensitivity reactions including rash and (rarely) angioedema
Acute-phase reaction (transient flu-like symptoms) - less common with oral bisphosphonates
emergency: Severe esophageal pain/dysphagia or GI bleeding
Acute thigh/groin pain suggesting impending atypical femoral fracture

monitoring: Serum calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D before starting and during treatment; correct deficiency
Bone mineral density (DXA) and bone turnover markers to assess response
Dental/oral examination before and during therapy; counsel on jaw symptoms
New thigh, hip, or groin pain (evaluate for atypical femoral fracture, including the opposite femur)
Upper-GI symptoms and adherence to administration instructions
counsel: Take this tablet first thing in the morning, before any food, drink, or other medicine
Swallow it whole with a full glass (about 180 mL) of plain water - do not chew or suck it
Stay sitting or standing upright for at least 30 minutes and do not lie down
Wait at least 30 minutes before eating, drinking anything else, or taking other medicines
Tell your doctor right away if you get new or worsening heartburn, chest pain, or trouble/pain swallowing
Keep up good dental hygiene and tell your dentist you take this medicine before any dental surgery
Report new thigh, hip, or groin pain promptly
Take your calcium and vitamin D as advised, but at a different time of day from this tablet
pk: Antiresorptive effect over weeks; bone turnover markers fall within weeks
Plasma Tmax within a few hours; exposure ~1.8-fold higher in the elderly
Prolonged terminal elimination with long skeletal retention (years); plasma elimination without accumulation on once-daily dosing
Long - allows once-daily or once-every-4-weeks dosing
Store at room temperature, protected from moisture, in original packaging (per Japanese label)
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - data are from the Japanese package insert (PMDA; Bonoteo/Recalbon) and published literature
Two interchangeable regimens: 1 mg once daily OR 50 mg once every 4 weeks
Strict administration: empty stomach, ~180 mL plain water, stay upright and fast 30 minutes - identical principles to other oral bisphosphonates
Food (especially high-fat) and polyvalent cations dramatically cut absorption - timing is critical
Correct hypocalcemia and vitamin D deficiency before and during therapy
Class risks: esophagitis, osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fracture - assess dental health and new thigh/groin pain
Renally eliminated - use caution in renal impairment and the elderly
missed: For the once-daily tablet: if you forget your morning dose, skip it for that day and take the next dose the following morning as usual - do not take it later in the day with food and do not double up. For the 50 mg once-every-4-weeks tablet: take it on the morning after you remember the missed dose, then resume taking it every 4 weeks from that new date. Never take two doses on the same day.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Oral overdose may cause upper-GI upset (nausea, heartburn, esophagitis/gastritis) and hypocalcemia. Give milk or calcium-containing antacids to bind the drug and reduce absorption; because of esophageal risk do not induce vomiting and keep the patient upright. Monitor and correct serum calcium; provide symptomatic and supportive care.
